source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: GPT-3 matched or beat UCLA undergraduates on a Raven-style digit matrix task, letter-string analogies, four-term verbal analogies and SAT analogies, with similar error patterns.
numbers: Digit matrices: humans N=40, GPT-3 better (generative OR=1.88, p=0.005; multiple choice OR=6.27). Letter strings: humans N=57, GPT-3 OR=1.76 overall; error profile correlated with humans r(39)=0.7. Verbal analogies N=57 (UCLA VAT); SAT items above the estimated high-school average.
limits: Zero-shot, short context. Humans were undergraduates, not top performers. Later work (c03, c04, c05) shows the letter-string result breaks on counterfactual alphabets. Training contamination cannot be ruled out.
agent_relevance: Baseline claim that plain LLMs can do relational mapping in-context when content is familiar. It is not proof that O7 works on unfamiliar structure.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) story analogies and Gick-Holyoak radiation probe (same paper)
finding: GPT-3 preferred the causally analogous story over a surface-matched story in the near case but was worse than students in the far case. GPT-4, tested briefly, did much better. On Duncker's radiation problem GPT-3 did not find the convergence solution alone, but did when the general-and-fortress story was in context and it was asked to use it.
numbers: Story analogies (Gentner materials): humans N=54, 15 of 54 chose the analogous story on every trial. GPT-3 vs humans OR=0.37, p=0.0003 (humans better). GPT-3 above chance in the near case (binomial p=0.0039). GPT-4 near perfect in near, strong in far (72 problems, ChatGPT interface, context cleared each time). Radiation: qualitative transcripts, no rate.
quote: when prompted to consider the previous stories, GPT-3 ... identified the general story as most relevant
limits: The radiation test is qualitative (one prompt set, no counts). With distractor stories GPT-3 did not pick the analog spontaneously; it needed an explicit prompt to consider prior stories. Authors note GPT-3 has no long-term memory, so retrieval is not tested.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM replication of Gick and Holyoak: mapping and transfer work once the analog is in context and flagged; spontaneous retrieval is the weak link. Supports O7 as an explicit step with the source supplied.

source: Hodel and West (2024) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Counterexample study on letter-string analogies: with a shuffled (synthetic) alphabet and bigger letter intervals, GPT-3 collapsed while students stayed high. They argue human tests do not validate a general zero-shot reasoner.
numbers: 121 UW undergraduates, 18 zero-generalisation items each (6 per setting). GPT-3 generative accuracy on the synthetic alphabet below 0.1 for extend, successor, predecessor and fix-alphabetic; only remove-redundant and sort stayed near original. Comprehension checks: GPT-3 handled the alphabet in most cases (at least 30 percent of original level, except predecessor on the synthetic alphabet). N=50 per GPT cell.
quote: GPT-3 fails to solve simplest variations of the original tasks, whereas human performance remains consistently high
limits: GPT-3 only. Webb et al. replied that failure reflects counting weakness, not missing analogy ability (see c05). Human sample from one university.
agent_relevance: Failed-replication evidence: relational mapping that looks good on familiar content is tied to memorised sequences. Test O7 on re-labelled, unfamiliar symbols before trusting it.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs (CogSci)
finding: Humans stayed steady across permuted and symbol alphabets; GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 dropped as more letters were permuted and dropped again on non-letter symbols. On the original alphabet GPT models were below the human average, unlike in Webb et al.
numbers: 136 Prolific participants (2 rejected). Mean accuracy over all alphabets and problem types (1,876 human samples, 6,840 per model): humans 0.753; the three models 0.488, 0.350, 0.452 (extraction of the table was garbled, so which value belongs to GPT-3, 3.5 or 4 should be checked). Comprehension checks: GPT-4 near 1.0 on successor and predecessor; GPT-3.5 weaker on predecessor in 2- and 5-letter permutations.
limits: Per-model assignment of the means is uncertain. Zero temperature. The prompt format of Hodel and West worked best.
agent_relevance: A clean test of whether the mapping rule is abstract. For our agent: check a mapping by code on a re-labelled instance (guardrail G10 style), not by accepting reasoning text.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in LLMs (extended version)
finding: Three domains of Webb et al. tested for robustness. Letter strings and digit-matrix blank position: GPT drops, humans do not. Digit-to-symbol swap: neither group changes. Story analogies: GPT-4 has a strong answer-order bias and loses more than humans when the correct story is paraphrased to remove sentence-level overlap with the source. Also reports Webb et al.'s reply: a GPT-4 with code execution wrote code mapping letters to indices and solved the shuffled-alphabet problems.
numbers: Story analogies, 18 far-analogy problems: GPT-4 (Webb data) 0.89 correct-first, 0.61 correct-second, 0.75 total; GPT-4 (new run) 1.0 / 0.72 / 0.86; humans 0.78 / 0.78 / 0.78 (720 items, 245 recruited, 5 rejected). Paraphrased correct story: GPT-4 0.86 to 0.72 (26/36); humans 0.78 to 0.70 (503/720). Two later GPT-4 versions did not beat 0613.
limits: Only 18 stories, so the paraphrase effect on GPT-4 is not shown significant. Humans also lost accuracy on paraphrase, so part of the original score came from surface overlap in the stimuli. The code-interpreter result is described second-hand with no rate.
agent_relevance: Surface overlap leaks into analogy tests. When our agent scores a mapping, vary answer order and paraphrase the source, and require the same mapping each time. The code-interpreter case supports splitting the work: the model proposes the rule, code executes and checks it, as in O7.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Millière, Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning (Journal of Memory and Language)
finding: Tasks that map word meaning onto symbol strings. GPT-4, Claude 3 Opus and Llama-405B match humans in default conditions; Claude 3 matches humans in every semantic-content condition; GPT-4 and Llama drop when the structure is generalised. LLMs are more distracted by irrelevant lexical items than humans.
numbers: 194 Brown students (132 structure, 62 content). Match to reference: humans 0.4 to 0.9; best LLMs 0.1 to 0.95. Weak models in Defaults: Pythia-12B 0.0, Falcon-40B 0.1, GPT-3 0.5, Claude 2 0.6. Distracted condition: all groups drop about 0.25. Semantic Content: GPT-4 about 0.7 in Categorial and Dual-attribute (humans 0.7 and 0.4) but 0.2 to 0.3 in Numeric conditions (significantly worse, p=0.001 and p=0.029). Claude 3 0.4 to 0.7, not different from humans.
limits: Match to reference, not accuracy. Quiz items accumulate in the prompt. Newer reasoning models not tested.
agent_relevance: Re-representing meaning into a new domain is feasible for strong models but fragile with numeric properties and distractors. Filter irrelevant source detail before mapping.

source: Sourati, Ilievski, Sommerauer, Jiang (2024) ARN: Analogical reasoning on narratives (TACL)
finding: Benchmark built on Gentner's near/far and relational/surface split. LLMs spot near analogies but fail on far analogies when the distractor shares surface features; GPT-4 scored below random there. Surface similarity (SBERT) acts as a trap.
numbers: 1,096 triples. Zero-shot accuracy (random 50, humans mean 96.0): GPT-4 (near analogy vs far distractor) 94.0, (near,near) 92.5, (far,far) 57.1, (far analogy vs near distractor) 29.1, mean 68.1. GPT-3.5 mean 60.3, 21.7 on far-vs-near. SBERT mean 42.3, 1.00 on far-vs-near. Humans 91.4 on far-vs-near. Few-shot with CoT (extract the proverbial message first): GPT models gained up to 30 absolute points on far analogies; CoT demos still hurt near analogies.
quote: even the largest ones struggle with far analogies in a zero-shot setting, with GPT4.0 scoring below random
limits: Narrative pairs with proverb-level messages; framework-generated with annotator checks. Plain few-shot demos hurt near analogies.
agent_relevance: Most direct match to systematicity: models are pulled by surface overlap. A scaffold step that first extracts the abstract message (the relational core), then compares, fixes much of the far case. Use for O7 retrieval and mapping check.

source: Jiayang et al. (2023) StoryAnalogy: story-level analogies from LLMs (EMNLP)
finding: Models often choose the surface-similar hard negative instead of the analogous story. A retrieval baseline built on structure-mapping ideas (clusters entities, finds mappings) resists hard negatives better than the LLMs.
numbers: Four-option multiple choice, random 25 percent, humans 85.7 percent. Text-davinci-003 about 37.1 percent, ChatGPT about 30 to 35, LLaMa-65B about 28 to 48 depending on prompt. Sultan and Shahaf structure-mapping-style baseline 44.9 percent. Best LLM 37.7 points below humans. Asking for a 'creative analogy', or giving the definition of structure mapping theory, beat the plain instruction.
limits: Table text partly garbled in extraction; only headline numbers used. 2023 models. A fine-tuned FlanT5-xxl matched zero-shot ChatGPT on generation.
agent_relevance: Putting the structure-mapping definition in the prompt gave a measurable lift: a cheap step to add when the agent compares analogues.

source: Ye, Wang et al. (2024) AnaloBench: identification of abstract and long-context analogies (EMNLP)
finding: Picking the analogous story gets harder as stories get longer; scale helps at one sentence but little for long stories. Retrieving analogues from a 200-story bank is near random for GPT-4 and Claude.
numbers: T1 accuracy at 1, 10, 30 sentences (random 25): GPT-4 89.1, 66.5, 60.7; GPT-3.5 65.3, 46.4, 30.8; Claude 68.2, 30.2, 25.9; Tulu2-70B 71.8, 51.2, 31.5; humans 96.0, 72.5, 73.3. GPT-4 gap to humans 6.9 points at 1 sentence, 28.8 at 30 sentences. T2 (200-story bank, top-10): both models near the random baseline, except GPT-4 Turbo with one-sentence stories. GPT-4 did as well on Claude-written stories (69.7 vs 66.5 at 10 sentences), so self-preference is not the cause.
limits: 340 human-written one-sentence analogies extended by GPT-4 into longer stories. No human data for T2.
agent_relevance: Retrieving a far analogue from a big pool is the failing step. Our agent should not depend on the model recalling a distant analogue from memory; give it a curated pool and rank by relational summaries.

source: Stevenson, Pafford, van der Maas, Mitchell (2026) Can large language models generalize analogy solving like children can? (TACL)
finding: Children, adults and LLMs solved letter-string analogies in Latin, Greek (near transfer) and symbol (far transfer) alphabets. Humans held their level; LLMs fell, most on the symbol alphabet.
numbers: Mean accuracy Latin / Greek / Symbol: adults 0.88 / 0.91 / 0.89 (n=62); children 0.62 / 0.66 / 0.67 (n=41); Claude-3.5 0.68 / 0.62 / 0.46; Gemma-2 27B 0.60 / 0.39 / 0.14; GPT-4o 0.85 / 0.63 / 0.48; Llama-3.1 405B 0.79 / 0.74 / 0.27 (54 runs each). GPT-4o and Llama-405B beat children in Latin. Five prompt templates tested.
limits: Letter strings only. No reasoning models in the list. Children recruited in the Netherlands.
agent_relevance: Strong LLMs beat children in the trained domain but not at transfer to a new domain. Transfer is the hard part; test O7 on far symbols, not familiar ones.

source: Puranam, Sen, Workiewicz (2025) Can LLMs help improve analogical reasoning for strategic decisions? Humans and GPT-4
finding: Gick and Holyoak style matching task with two source stories and two target problems. GPT-4 did not spontaneously use the correct source. With a hint that an analogy exists, GPT-4 used it every time but also claimed the wrong story about half the time. Humans claimed fewer analogies but were more often right.
numbers: Humans n=199, GPT-4 n=60 runs. No hint: GPT-4 precision 0.00, recall 0.00, accuracy 0.50 on both problems; humans precision 0.42 and 1.00, recall 0.06 and 0.22. With hint: GPT-4 recall 1.00, precision 0.50 to 0.52, F1 0.67 to 0.68; humans precision 0.67 to 0.75, recall 0.26 to 0.39, F1 0.38 to 0.51, accuracy 57 to 63 percent. Human solve rate: HR problem 37 percent (17/46) with hint vs 20.3 percent without; factory 8.7 vs 6.3 percent. Original Gick and Holyoak 1983 Exp 2: 29 percent (8/28) vs 50 percent (14/28) with hint. GPT-4 used an analogy on the factory problem 1/15 times without hint, 15/15 with hint.
limits: One model (GPT-4), business-case problems, preprint. Authors note a demand effect: the hint makes the LLM over-claim. Human solve rates lower than in the original study, partly due to the matching load.
agent_relevance: Key warning: given a pool of sources, an LLM over-applies analogies. O7 needs a verifier that checks causal correspondences before transfer, and an explicit no-analogy option.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (ICLR)
finding: Analogical prompting: the model first recalls relevant problems and knowledge, then solves. Beats 0-shot CoT and manual few-shot CoT on math, code and BIG-Bench, with gains strongest for larger models.
numbers: Reported average gain +4 percent. Codeforces, GPT-3.5-turbo Acc@1: 15 percent with self-generated knowledge plus exemplars vs 16 percent for GPT-4 baseline. K=3 or 5 exemplars best; K=1 underperforms (MATH 34.8 at K=1 vs 37.3 at K=4, GPT-3.5). Manual check of 100 cases: in 35 of 50 correct cases exemplars were relevant and correct; in 28 of 50 wrong cases exemplars were good but the model failed to generalise (12 generalisation gap, 8 over-reliance on one exemplar).
limits: Mostly near, same-domain recall, not distant analogy. On weaker models retrieved exemplars beat self-generated ones. More output tokens. Sensitive to prompt wording.
agent_relevance: Cheapest LLM-loop use of analogical recall. Treat it as near analogy only; it does not test structure mapping.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) same paper: scale boundary
finding: Self-generated analogues help only when the model is strong enough. With small models, exemplars retrieved from labelled data win.
numbers: GSM8K, text-davinci family: self-generated exemplars beat fixed 5-shot CoT at text-davinci-002 and -003 but not at text-curie-001 or text-davinci-001. Table values (column assignment inferred from a garbled table): fixed 5-shot CoT 43 and 50 percent, retrieved 47 and 54, self-generated 48 and 61 at the two larger models.
limits: Table columns hard to read; only the direction is firm.
agent_relevance: Do not add self-generated analogues for a weak base model. Gate O7 on model strength.

source: Yu et al. (2024) Thought Propagation: an analogical approach to complex reasoning with LLMs (ICLR)
finding: Solve several analogous sub-problems and aggregate their solutions into the answer to the input problem. Improves optimal shortest paths, creative-writing coherence and ALFWorld completion.
numbers: Shortest path optimal rate, 0-shot: GPT-3.5 TP 0.65 vs IO 0.33, CoT 0.26, ToT 0.22; GPT-4 TP 0.88 vs IO 0.78; PaLM-2 TP 0.36 vs CoT 0.24. 100 shortest-path items. Creative writing (100 prompts): coherence GPT-4 7.989 vs ToT 7.684 and CoT 6.927; human preference 45 percent vs 33 (ToT) and 15 (CoT). ALFWorld (134 environments): TP variants 82 to 95 percent vs Reflexion 79.1; best 94.78. Abstract claims average +12 percent shortest path, +13 percent writing preference, +15 percent ALFWorld.
limits: The 'analogous problems' are neighbour sub-problems or rephrasings of the input, not distant domains. ToT fails in some settings, which flatters TP. Some ALFWorld baselines quoted from other papers.
agent_relevance: A working agent-loop pattern: generate analogues, solve each, aggregate. It tests near analogy and decomposition, so do not cite it as evidence for far-analogue transfer.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners (AAAI)
finding: Agent stores past trajectories, extracts rule-like insights, and at test time retrieves similar past tasks as few-shot examples (case-based reasoning). Both parts help, and insights transferred across tasks.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieve-only success: HotpotQA 36 vs 31 percent, ALFWorld 50 vs 55 percent, WebShop 37 vs 38 percent. ALFWorld retrieve-only 40.3 to 54.4 percent over Reflexion rounds R0 to R3; ExpeL plus Reflexion 54.5 to 60.4, a variant up to 64.2. Transfer HotpotQA to FEVER: ReAct 58 percent, ExpeL transfer variants 63 (without task demos) to 70 percent.
limits: Retrieval is by task-description similarity, so it is near analogy. Some transfer rows were unlabeled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Near-analogy retrieval plus abstracted insights adds value in agent loops. The abstracted insights are what move across tasks.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts: thought-augmented reasoning with LLMs (NeurIPS)
finding: Stores abstract thought-templates distilled from solved problems, retrieves the nearest for a new problem and instantiates it. This is schema-based analogy in an agent loop. Large gains on a few puzzle tasks.
numbers: Game of 24: BoT 82.4 percent vs ToT 74.0 and GPT-4 3.0. Checkmate-in-One: 86.4 vs next best 57.2. Claims +11 percent Game of 24, +20 percent Geometric Shapes, +51 percent Checkmate-in-One over previous best; about 12 percent of multi-query cost; Llama3-8B plus BoT may rival Llama3-70B.
limits: Gains concentrate on tasks with a repeated structural template (puzzles). Template retrieval is by embedding similarity. Authors' own comparisons; no independent replication seen in this search.
agent_relevance: A schema store gives large gains where problems share structure. Fits O7 plus S4 harvesting: keep abstracted templates, not raw traces.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Take a step back: evoking reasoning via abstraction (ICLR)
finding: Ask the model first for the underlying principle (abstraction), then solve. It is the 'extract the relational core' step of structure mapping without a second case.
numbers: PaLM-2L: MMLU Physics +7 percent, Chemistry +11 percent, TimeQA +27 percent, MuSiQue +7 percent (abstract).
limits: Only the abstract was read; error analysis not checked. Not a two-case mapping.
agent_relevance: A one-line prompt that approximates schema induction; cheap to add before O7.

source: Bhavya, Xiong, Zhai (2022) Analogy generation by prompting LLMs: a case study of InstructGPT
finding: InstructGPT can write analogies for science concepts. Precise imperative prompts at low temperature work best; question prompts and typos hurt. Only the largest model reached human level when free to pick any analogy.
numbers: Share of analogies rated meaningful (3 raters each, 1,407 analogies; Fleiss kappa 0.35 with source, 0.55 without): no-source task 1.90, 15.61, 48.29, 70.05 percent for 0.3B, 1.3B, 6.7B, 175B vs humans 66.67. With a given source: 8.97, 29.05, 38.46, 53.79 vs humans 71.88.
limits: Explaining a given source-target pair (needs mapping) was worse than free generation, so the free-generation score may reflect memorised analogies. Science concepts only.
agent_relevance: Free-form analogue generation looks strong, but explaining a specified mapping is weaker; check the mapping, not just that an analogue exists.

source: Ding, Srinivasan, MacNeil, Chan (2023) Fluid transformers and creative analogies (C&C)
finding: GPT-3 produced cross-domain analogies for design problems. A one-shot prompt using the Duncker radiation example made outputs more useful and less similar to the input problem than zero-shot. People rated them helpful for reformulating problems.
numbers: 480 analogies from six design problems over four runs. One-shot judged potentially useful 80 percent vs zero-shot 40 percent; similarity to input below 0.5 vs above 0.7. Few-shot 67 percent useful, similarity about 0.3. About 70 percent unique and useful in the best prompt. Study 2 (Prolific, US): median helpfulness 4 of 5; about 80 percent of cases changed problem formulations; up to 25 percent of outputs rated potentially harmful, mostly upsetting content.
limits: Usefulness is a rater judgement, not solution quality. Duplicates high for some problems. Task was reformulation, not final solving.
agent_relevance: A worked far-analogy example in the prompt raises both distance and usefulness. A good seed for open-mode analogue prompts.

source: Mitchell, Palmarini, Moskvichev (2023) Comparing humans, GPT-4 and GPT-4V on abstraction and reasoning tasks (ConceptARC)
finding: On concept-based abstraction (rule transfer by analogy), GPT-4 text and GPT-4V stay far below humans, even with a richer one-shot prompt.
numbers: ConceptARC 480 tasks: humans 91 percent, first-place Kaggle program 52 percent, GPT-4 25 percent in the first study. A detailed one-shot prompt raised GPT-4 to 0.33 (from 0.19 and 0.25 zero-shot). Minimal tasks (48): humans 0.95, GPT-4 text 0.69 and 0.65, GPT-4V 0.25 zero-shot and 0.23 one-shot.
limits: ARC-style grid tasks, only loosely structure mapping. 2023 models; current reasoning models not in this paper.
agent_relevance: Abstract rule transfer from a few examples was weak for 2023 models; confirm on current models before assuming O7 helps on grid puzzles.

source: Opiełka et al. (2025) Analogical reasoning inside LLMs: concept vectors and the limits of abstraction
finding: Inside Llama-3.1, concept vectors for verbal concepts like antonym stay stable across input format, but no stable vector for abstract 'previous/next'. This matches the letter-string failure: alphabet-specific memory, not a shared abstraction.
numbers: Llama-3.1 70B letter-string accuracy by permuted letters: 0.35 (none), 0.10 (2), 0.05 (5), 0.00 (10), 0.00 (20), 0.15 (symbols); chance 0.04 letters, 0.1 symbols. Previous/next: 98 percent on known lists vs 62 percent in the abstract version. 600 in-context prompts analysed.
limits: Open-weight models only; linear-representation assumption. A correct internal representation may still give a wrong output.
agent_relevance: Mechanistic support for brittle mapping. A reason to verify mappings externally rather than trust the model's stated rule.

source: Yuan et al. (2024) AnalogyKB: a million-scale analogy knowledge base from knowledge graphs (ACL)
finding: A knowledge base of same-relation and analogous-relation analogies, filtered by LLM and humans, lifts small models on analogy recognition to near human level. Skipping the quality check removes the gain.
numbers: Mean over six datasets (E-KAR, BATS, UNIT2, UNIT4, Google, SAT): RoBERTa-large 59.92 baseline, 77.44 with AnalogyKB, 58.08 with unchecked data. DeBERTa-v3 62.03 to 78.11 (59.64 unchecked). Human mean 78.87.
limits: Word-pair and relation analogies, multiple choice; training on benchmark-like data, so not a test of spontaneous analogy.
agent_relevance: Quality-checked relational data is what moves analogy skill; unchecked machine-made analogies add nothing. Argues for a verification step in any analogy store.

source: Wijesiriwardene et al. (2023) ANALOGICAL: benchmark for long-text analogy in LLMs
finding: Six-level analogy taxonomy (word, word vs sentence, syntactic, negation, entailment, metaphor), tested on embeddings of eight LLMs. Identifying analogies gets harder up the taxonomy.
numbers: Thirteen datasets, three distance measures, eight LLMs. Exact scores not extracted.
limits: Embedding-distance proxy rather than prompted reasoning. Only abstract and structure read.
agent_relevance: Low weight; embedding similarity alone is a poor proxy for relational match.

source: Camposampiero et al. (2025) Can large reasoning models do analogical reasoning under perceptual uncertainty? (I-RAVEN-X)
finding: Search snippet: o3-mini and DeepSeek-R1 do well on Raven-type analogy with clean symbols but drop sharply once perception is uncertain.
numbers: Snippet gives R1 falling from 80.6 to 23.2 percent with 3.4x more reasoning tokens; fragmentary, unverified.
limits: Not opened; only a search snippet from an aggregator page.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models may still be brittle in mapping under noise; check before relying.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu reply (2024) to critics, code-interpreter GPT-4 (not opened)
finding: The Nature page of the original paper came up in search; the reply itself was not opened. Content known only through the description in c05.
numbers: None read directly.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Use c05 for the claim; verify before citing the reply as a primary source.

source: Reimplementation and Reinterpretation of the Copycat Project (arXiv listing, 2018; not opened)
finding: Copycat is the older computational system for letter-string analogy (Hofstadter and Mitchell), built from a slipnet and a coderack, a non-LLM way to build mappings. Only the paper's title was seen in an arXiv listing.
numbers: None read.
limits: Only a title seen; arXiv id not confirmed.
agent_relevance: Older computational baseline for letter-string analogies; a fair comparator for LLM results on the same items.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) counterfactual study: prompt effects and reading of results
finding: Prompt choice mattered less than alphabet change. Of several prompts tried, the Hodel and West wording ('Use this fictional alphabet:') gave the best results across models, yet all GPT models still dropped on permuted and symbol alphabets.
numbers: Baseline on Webb's zero-generalisation items: results similar to Webb for GPT-3 but with notable differences on Predecessor and Fix-Alphabet, and lower for GPT-4 on Remove-Redundant and Sort. Samples per cell 420 for alphabets n=0 to 20 and 40 for symbols for GPT models; human cells 268 to 384.
limits: Zero temperature only; no chain-of-thought variants reported in the part read.
agent_relevance: Prompt engineering did not rescue the transfer failure; scaffolding must add a check, not only a better wording.

source: Puranam et al. (2025) matching framing versus Gick-Holyoak retrieval
finding: Frames matching (choosing which source fits which target) as a separate stage from retrieval. Humans in the original study got a lone source; with two sources and two targets human solve rates fell.
numbers: Original Gick and Holyoak (1983, Exp 2): 29 percent (8/28) solved unhinted, 50 percent (14/28) hinted. This study (n=199, two stories, two problems): 6.3 and 20.3 percent unhinted, 8.7 and 37 percent hinted.
limits: Different materials and population (business students), so the drop mixes matching load with stimulus difficulty.
agent_relevance: Evidence that choosing among several candidate analogues is a hard step; O7 should compare candidates against each other, not use the first retrieved.
